query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of interstitial carbon during alloy synthesis will promote the in‐situ formation of finely dispersed, coherent carbide precipitates along the lamellar colony interfaces, thereby strengthening the interface against microcrack initiation while simultaneously providing additional dislocation pinning that enhances strain hardening. This combined effect is expected to improve both the tensile strength and ductility at room temperature relative to the unmodified eutectic HEA.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., an AlCoCrFeNi2.1‐type alloy) made by casting that forms dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, which in its as‐cast state shows limited room-temperature ductility due to microcrack initiation along the unmodified interfaces.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low (trace) concentration of interstitial carbon into the alloy during synthesis so that during solidification and subsequent thermo‐mechanical processing a population of nanoscale, coherent carbide precipitates preferentially forms at lamellar interfaces.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing; the carbon content must remain very low (e.g., below ~0.1 wt%) to avoid coarse, brittle carbide formation; processing routes (casting + controlled thermo‐mechanical treatment) identical to the baseline alloy aside from the carbon addition.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoscale carbide precipitates (or carbon-rich interfacial particles) that decorate the lamellar colony boundaries and phase interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The interfacial carbides are expected to improve cohesion at the phase boundaries by impeding crack nucleation and propagation, while also acting as obstacles to dislocation motion. This dual action should raise the yield and ultimate tensile strengths (via precipitation/dislocation strengthening) and promote a more progressive strain hardening behavior that delays failure, thereby enhancing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar microstructure, the carbon-modified alloy should exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths as well as increased total elongation under room-temperature tensile loading, with evidence of improved strain hardening and delayed microcrack formation at the lamellar interfaces.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with as-cast dual-phase lamellar colonies that, while strong, suffers from premature microcrack initiation at its numerous internal boundaries and consequent limited ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The positive effects are expected only if the carbon level is kept low enough to form a fine dispersion of coherent carbides without leading to the formation of coarse, embrittling carbides. The intervention is primarily targeted at improving room-temperature properties; its influence at elevated temperatures is not part of this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty regarding the optimal carbon level required to obtain the desired nanoscale carbide precipitates and their uniform distribution along all critical interfaces, as well as the precise balance between improved dislocation pinning and avoiding the formation of brittle phases. Detailed process optimization may be needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the same eutectic HEA using identical casting and thermo-mechanical processing parameters. One batch (the test group) is synthesized with a trace addition of carbon (e.g., <0.1 wt%), while the other batch (the control) is made without carbon. After ensuring similar microstructural evolution aside from the expected interfacial carbide formation, perform room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests and detailed microstructural analyses (using TEM/SEM) focusing on the lamellar interfaces.
measurements: Observation of the carbide precipitate size, distribution, and coherence at lamellar interfaces
Fractography to assess crack initiation and propagation paths
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-added samples do not exhibit statistically significant increases in both tensile strength and ductility (e.g., no improvement or a deterioration compared to the control) or if microstructural analysis reveals that the carbon addition yields coarse, inhomogeneous, or non-coherent carbide precipitates that lead to earlier crack initiation, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The excellent tensile properties of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy at cryogenic temperatures are mainly caused by deformation twinning,,. However, such twinning is difficult to achieve at room temperature because the resolved shear stress is insufficient to reach the critical stress for twinning,. Another issue is the relatively low yield strength (0.2–0.6 GPa) caused by the fcc structural characteristics of the alloy,,,,. Here, we effectively induce twinning in an HEA at room temperature and exploit the induced twinning to improve the cryogenic tensile properties, particularly the yield strength, of the material. Recently, new types of dual-phase high entropy alloys (HEAs) were designed under the inspiration of second phase strengthening, showing good combination of high fracture strength and tensile ductility at room temperature,. In contrast to the conventional strategies for alloy design, HEAs are developed with at least five metallic elements, emerging as a new frontier of research in recent years. The chemically disordered distributions of multiple elements in HEAs have been suggested to show important influence on dislocation slip,. In particularly, the high mixture of multiple elements in dual-phase HEAs may form distinctive phase boundary structures compared to conventional ones, which could result in different influence on dislocation behaviors. However, experimental observation and analysis are still lacking for a profound understanding of the deformation mechanisms of dual-phase HEAs.
